summary: Teach generating equivalent fractions as a procedure grounded in re-partitioning the same quantity: splitting each part of a model into n gives n times as many parts, each 1/n the size, so the amount is unchanged — mirrored numerically as multiplying numerator and denominator by n. Work both directions (build up and simplify by dividing out a common factor), complete equivalence chains, and always pair the numeric move with 'why is it the same amount?' on a diagram to head off the additive error (adding the same number to top and bottom).
misconceptions: Additive equivalence — add the same number to top and bottom (1/3 → 2/4) — whole-number thinking (IES)
Changing only one part — doubling the numerator but not the denominator
Simplifying by subtracting a common number rather than dividing
Counting parts mechanically without checking the amount is unchanged

activities.title: Re-partition a bar to build equivalent fractions
steps: Start with a bar showing 1/3: one of three equal parts shaded.
Split each part into 2 and recount: the bar now shows 2/6, but the shaded LENGTH is unchanged.
Write the numeric move alongside the picture: ×2 on the top and ×2 on the bottom, 1/3 = 2/6.
Repeat splitting each part into 3 and into 4 to generate 3/9 and 4/12, each time checking the shaded length stays the same.
Deliberately test 'add 1 to each' (1/3 → 2/4): redraw 2/4 and compare its shaded length to 1/3 — it is longer, so the amount changed.
Build a simplify version: group the parts of 4/8 into equal groups and divide both counts by the common factor to reach 1/2, checking the shaded amount is unchanged.
activities.insight: Multiplying both numerator and denominator by the same whole number greater than 1, or dividing both by a common factor greater than 1, re-partitions the SAME amount into more (or fewer) equal parts, so the value is preserved; adding the same non-zero number to both changes the amount (except for a fraction equal to one whole, such as 2/2 → 3/3).

activities.title: Complete equivalence chains and simplify both directions
steps: Fill in the blanks in a chain: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12, stating the multiplier used from 1/4 to reach each fraction (×2 for eighths, ×3 for twelfths).
Complete 2/5 = ?/10 = ?/20 and describe the pattern in the numerators and denominators.
Simplify 4/8 to its simplest form; then try dividing by 2 first and compare — do you reach the same simplest form?
Sort or match a set of fractions into 'equivalent to 1/3' and 'not equivalent', explaining each decision.
Answer 'which is 1/3 written in sixths?' and explain why an additive answer like 2/4 is wrong.
activities.insight: Equivalence is reversible and multiplicative: the same quantity has infinitely many equivalent names, and building up (×n) and simplifying (÷ common factor) are the same relationship run in opposite directions.

activities.title: Explain and defend the rule
steps: After making 1/3 into 2/6 by ×2, explain on the strip WHY that keeps the value the same.
Judge a claim: 'Jo made 1/3 into 2/4 by adding one to each' — is Jo right? Show why or why not on a model.
State the rule you used in your own words and test it on one new example of your choice.
activities.insight: A correct equivalence method can be justified on a diagram and distinguished from the additive error through reasoning, not just by recalling 'do the same to both'.

checkQuestion: Here is 1/3 shown on an area model and a fraction strip. Task: make three different fractions that are equal to 1/3, showing each on the model, and tell me the rule you used. Then simplify 4/8 to its simplest form, and complete this chain: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12. I'll watch how you work.
checkAnswer: Generates e.g. 2/6, 3/9, 4/12 by splitting each third into equal parts / multiplying top and bottom by the same number, each shown as the same shaded amount; simplifies 4/8 → 1/2 by dividing both by 4; completes 1/4 = 2/8 = 3/12.
